meta.subject: CHINESE
meta.author: bank-team-chinese
meta.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.topic: Why twelve months fall short of a year
questions.learningObjective: Explain why twelve lunar months fall short of a solar year
questions.stem: Why do twelve lunar months fall short of a solar year?

options.text: Because twelve lunar months total about 354 days
Because lunar months are longer than solar months
Because the sun moves faster than the moon
options.misconception: confuses orbital speeds with month length

options.text: Because years contain only ten months

questions.explanation: Twelve lunar months total about 354 days, short of 365. The tempting reversal answer gets the comparison backwards.

questions.topic: How the length of a lunar month is obtained
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a lunar month's length is obtained
questions.stem: How is the length of a lunar month obtained?

answer.exemplar: A lunar month is obtained by measuring the interval between successive identical phases, such as new moon to new moon, which averages about 29.53 days.

questions.explanation: The month spans one full phase cycle. The tempting fixed-30-days answer ignores the measured average.

questions.topic: The nineteen-year cycle of months
questions.stem: What does the nineteen-year cycle of months accomplish?

options.text: It makes every month exactly 30 days
It aligns lunar months with the solar year over 19 years
It shortens the year to 354 days

questions.explanation: The cycle realigns lunar and solar years. The tempting elimination answer reverses its purpose.

questions.topic: Leap months in one cycle
questions.learningObjective: Count leap months in a cycle
questions.stem: In a nineteen-year cycle, about how many leap months occur?
questions.explanation: Seven leap months keep the cycle aligned. The tempting twelve answer ignores the shortfall.

questions.topic: Why an eight-year cycle fails
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an eight-year cycle fails
questions.stem: Why does an eight-year cycle fail to align the calendars?

options.text: Because eight years is too short for drift to matter
Because the accumulated error remains too large

questions.explanation: Drift accumulates beyond tolerance in eight years. The tempting too-short answer underestimates error.

questions.topic: How long a month can be
questions.learningObjective: State how long a month can be
questions.stem: How long can a lunar month be?

options.misconception: treats a month as four weeks
confuses lunar month with calendar month

questions.explanation: Lunar months run 29 or 30 days. The tempting 28-day answer confuses weeks with months.

questions.topic: How long a year with a leap month is
questions.stem: A lunar year with one leap month has about how many days?
questions.explanation: Thirteen months of about 29.5 days total about 384 days. The tempting 365 answer ignores the leap month.

questions.topic: The day a lunar month begins
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a lunar month begins
questions.stem: On which day does a lunar month begin?

options.text: On the last day of the previous month

questions.explanation: Months begin at new moon. The tempting full-moon answer confuses start with midpoint.

questions.topic: Why the full moon falls near the fifteenth
questions.stem: Why does the full moon fall near the fifteenth?

answer.exemplar: The full moon falls near the fifteenth because the month begins at new moon and the full moon arrives about half a month later, roughly fourteen to fifteen days into the month.

questions.explanation: Full moon is about half a month after new moon. The tempting coincidence answer ignores the phase cycle.

questions.topic: Where the sixty-name cycle comes from
questions.learningObjective: Explain the origin of the sixty-name cycle
questions.stem: Where does the sixty-name cycle come from?

options.text: From a single list of sixty gods
From sixty years of a reign
From the sixty days of a month
From pairing ten stems with twelve branches

questions.explanation: The cycle pairs stems and branches. The tempting sixty-gods answer invents a false origin.

questions.topic: Why one hundred and twenty pairings give sixty names
questions.stem: Why do 120 stem-branch pairings give only 60 names?

options.text: Because only pairs of matching parity survive
Because half the pairings are discarded at random
Because stems and branches are equal in number
Because the cycle is actually 120 names

questions.explanation: Only same-parity pairs occur. The tempting random-discard answer treats reduction as arbitrary.

questions.topic: A name that comes round again after sixty years
questions.stem: Why does a cycle name return after sixty years?

answer.exemplar: A cycle name returns after sixty years because the least common multiple of ten stems and twelve branches is sixty, so both sequences realign only then.

questions.explanation: The LCM of 10 and 12 is 60. The tempting coincidence answer ignores the arithmetic.

questions.topic: Naming a modern year in the cycle
questions.learningObjective: Apply the cycle to a modern year
questions.stem: To name a modern year in the cycle, what do you need?

options.text: A reference year and its cycle name

questions.explanation: You need a reference point. The tempting number-only answer ignores the offset.

questions.topic: The cycle name of a revolution year
questions.learningObjective: Identify a revolution year's cycle name

stimulus.body: A chronology lists 1911 as the year a revolution ended imperial rule and 1949 as the founding of a republic, both named in the sixty-name cycle.

questions.stem: How can two such years share or differ in cycle names?

options.text: They must share the same name
They always differ by exactly one
They differ unless 38 years is a multiple of 60

questions.explanation: Names differ unless the gap is a multiple of 60. The tempting same-name answer ignores the 38-year gap.

questions.topic: The cycle name shared by two twentieth-century years
questions.stem: Two twentieth-century years share a cycle name if their difference is a multiple of 60. If one is 1924, what is the next sharing year?
questions.explanation: Adding 60 to 1924 gives 1984. The tempting 1954 answer adds only 30.

questions.topic: The branches as two-hour periods
questions.stem: What do the twelve branches represent as time periods?
questions.explanation: Branches mark two-hour periods. The tempting months-only answer confuses branch roles.

questions.topic: How the twelve periods fill a day
questions.learningObjective: Check how periods fill a day
questions.stem: Twelve two-hour periods fill how many hours of a day?
questions.explanation: Twelve times two equals twenty-four. The tempting twelve answer forgets to multiply.

questions.topic: The animal attached to each branch
questions.stem: Why is an animal attached to each branch?

options.text: As a mnemonic for the twelve branches

questions.explanation: Animals aid memory. The tempting creation answer invents myth.

questions.topic: The branches as month names
questions.stem: How can branches serve as month names?

options.text: They cannot, since branches are only for hours
Each branch names a lunar month in sequence

questions.explanation: Branches also name months in sequence. The tempting hours-only answer denies a secondary use.

questions.topic: Why the twenty-four terms are fifteen degrees apart
questions.learningObjective: Explain the 15-degree spacing of solar terms
questions.stem: Why are the twenty-four solar terms fifteen degrees apart?

answer.exemplar: The twenty-four terms are fifteen degrees apart because the full circle of 360 degrees divided by 24 terms gives 15 degrees, evenly spacing the sun's annual path.

questions.explanation: 360 divided by 24 equals 15. The tempting arbitrary-spacing answer ignores the division.

questions.topic: How far apart the solar terms fall
questions.stem: If solar terms are 15 degrees apart on the ecliptic, how many days roughly separate adjacent terms?
questions.explanation: Fifteen degrees is about half a month, roughly 15 days. The tempting 30 answer doubles the spacing.

questions.topic: The four terms fixed by the sun's position
questions.stem: Which four terms are fixed by the sun's position?

options.text: The four quarter days of the year

questions.explanation: Solstices and equinoxes fix four terms. The tempting arbitrary answer ignores astronomy.

questions.topic: Terms by an average sun against terms by the true sun
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish average and true sun terms
questions.stem: What is the difference between terms by an average sun and terms by the true sun?

options.text: There is no difference at all
True sun terms are always later by a year
Average sun terms are evenly spaced; true sun terms follow actual position

questions.explanation: Average sun terms are even; true sun terms follow reality. The tempting no-difference answer denies the distinction.

questions.topic: Seventy-two pentads of five days
questions.stem: What are the seventy-two pentads?

options.text: Five-day periods within the solar terms

questions.explanation: Pentads are five-day periods. The tempting months answer mislabels them.

questions.topic: The three periods of greatest heat
questions.stem: What are the three periods of greatest heat?
questions.explanation: Sanfu names the three hottest periods. The tempting random answer ignores the term.

questions.topic: Nine periods of nine days from the solstice
questions.stem: What do the nine periods of nine days from the solstice track?

answer.exemplar: The nine periods of nine days from the solstice track the gradual change in temperature and daylight, counting nine-day intervals after the winter or summer solstice.

questions.explanation: They count post-solstice intervals. The tempting arbitrary answer ignores the solstice anchor.

questions.topic: Which month becomes the leap month
questions.stem: Which month becomes a leap month?

options.misconception: fixes the leap month at year end

options.text: The month lacking a principal solar term
The month with two full moons
options.misconception: confuses blue moon with leap month

questions.explanation: The leap month lacks a principal term. The tempting fixed-month answer ignores the rule.

questions.topic: Why the calendar is not a lunar one
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the calendar is not purely lunar
questions.stem: Why is this calendar not a purely lunar one?

options.text: Because it ignores the moon entirely
Because it uses only solar months
Because solar terms anchor it to the sun

questions.explanation: Solar terms anchor the calendar to the sun. The tempting ignores-moon answer denies its lunar basis.

questions.topic: How often the new year falls in January
questions.learningObjective: State how often the new year falls in January
questions.stem: How often does the lunar new year fall in January?
questions.explanation: The new year shifts, landing in January about a third of the time. The tempting every-year answer ignores drift.

questions.topic: The range of new year dates
questions.learningObjective: State the range of new year dates
questions.stem: What is the range of possible lunar new year dates?

options.misconception: confuses lunar with solar new year

questions.explanation: The new year falls between 21 January and 20 February. The tempting fixed-date answer ignores variation.

questions.topic: Reign titles and the numbering of years
questions.learningObjective: Explain reign titles and year numbering
questions.stem: How are years numbered under a reign title?

options.text: By the animal of the year
By the year of the current reign title

questions.explanation: Years are numbered by reign title. The tempting age answer confuses reign with lifespan.

questions.topic: Counting years from the founding of a republic
questions.stem: How does counting years from a republic's founding differ from reign titles?

answer.exemplar: Counting from a republic's founding uses a fixed secular epoch instead of changing reign titles, so year numbers stay stable across governments.

questions.explanation: Republican counting uses a fixed epoch. The tempting same-as-reign answer ignores the shift to secular numbering.

questions.topic: The two halves of the rat period
questions.learningObjective: Describe the two halves of the rat period
questions.stem: What are the two halves of the rat period?

options.text: Early and late rat, split at midnight

options.misconception: confuses time of day with year

questions.explanation: The rat period splits at midnight. The tempting unrelated-animals answer confuses halves with branches.

questions.topic: One clock time across many local suns
questions.learningObjective: Explain one clock time across longitudes
questions.stem: What problem arises from using one clock time across many longitudes?

options.misconception: confuses time zones with lunar phases

options.text: Local sun time no longer matches clock time

questions.explanation: Clock time diverges from local sun time. The tempting no-problem answer ignores longitude.

questions.topic: The year measured against the stars
questions.stem: What is the year measured against the stars?

answer.exemplar: The year measured against the stars is the sidereal year, the time for the sun to return to the same position relative to the fixed stars, slightly longer than the tropical year.

questions.explanation: The sidereal year uses fixed stars. The tempting identical-to-tropical answer ignores precession.

questions.topic: Branches six apart as opposites
questions.stem: Why are branches six apart considered opposites?

options.text: Because six is the total number of branches
Because they share the same animal
Because they occur in the same hour
Because six is half of twelve

questions.explanation: Six is half of twelve, placing branches opposite. The tempting same-animal answer confuses opposite with identical.

questions.topic: The four groups of combining branches
questions.learningObjective: Describe the four groups of combining branches
questions.stem: How many groups of combining branches are there?
questions.explanation: There are four groups. The tempting two answer undercounts.

questions.topic: The six pairs of uniting branches
questions.learningObjective: Describe the six pairs of uniting branches
questions.stem: How many pairs of uniting branches are there?
questions.explanation: There are six pairs. The tempting four answer confuses with groups.

questions.topic: The ten stems and the five elements
questions.stem: How do the ten stems relate to the five elements?
questions.explanation: Two stems map to each element. The tempting one-per-element answer undercounts.

questions.topic: The order of the heavenly stems
questions.learningObjective: State the order of the heavenly stems
questions.stem: What is the order of the heavenly stems based on?
questions.explanation: Stems follow a fixed traditional sequence. The tempting random answer ignores tradition.

questions.topic: Why twelve months fall short of a year
questions.learningObjective: Apply the shortfall to a calendar
questions.stem: Given the 11-day shortfall, what must a lunar calendar do?
questions.explanation: Leap months correct the drift. The tempting do-nothing answer ignores accumulating error.

questions.topic: How the length of a lunar month is obtained

stimulus.body: A text says lunar months are always exactly 29 days, ignoring the half-day remainder and variation between months.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: No, because months vary between 29 and 30 days
Yes, because the moon is regular

questions.explanation: Months vary between 29 and 30 days. The tempting fixed-29 answer ignores variation.

questions.topic: The nineteen-year cycle of months
questions.stem: If you know a new moon date this year, how does the 19-year cycle help?

options.text: It does not help at all
It predicts similar new moons 19 years later

questions.explanation: The cycle predicts similar new moons 19 years later. The tempting 8-year answer confuses cycles.

questions.topic: Leap months in one cycle

stimulus.body: A table claims 12 leap months occur in 19 years, implying one leap month every 1.6 years.

questions.stem: Is this claim plausible?

options.text: Yes, because 12 leap months fit well
No, because leap months never occur
Yes, because more leap months means better accuracy
No, because about 7 leap months is expected

questions.explanation: About 7 leap months is expected. The tempting 12 answer overcounts intercalation.

questions.topic: Why an eight-year cycle fails
questions.stem: If an eight-year cycle is used, what happens over decades?
questions.explanation: Error accumulates and seasons drift. The tempting sufficiency answer underestimates drift.

questions.topic: How long a month can be
questions.stem: Why can a lunar month not be exactly 28 days?

answer.exemplar: A lunar month cannot be exactly 28 days because the measured phase cycle averages about 29.53 days, so 28 days would cut the cycle short and misalign phases.

questions.explanation: The phase cycle averages 29.53 days. The tempting 28-day answer ignores measurement.

questions.topic: How long a year with a leap month is
questions.stem: How does a leap year compare to a common lunar year?

options.text: It is longer by about 29 days

questions.explanation: A leap year adds about 29 days. The tempting shorter answer reverses the difference.

questions.topic: The day a lunar month begins
questions.stem: If the new moon occurs on 3 March, when does the lunar month begin?
questions.explanation: The month begins on the new moon. The tempting 15 March answer confuses start with full moon.

questions.topic: Why the full moon falls near the fifteenth

stimulus.body: A text claims the full moon always falls exactly on the fifteenth day of every lunar month without exception.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: No, because month length varies 29-30 days
Yes, because the moon is perfectly regular
No, because full moons never occur

questions.explanation: Month length varies 29-30 days, so timing shifts. The tempting exact-fifteenth answer ignores variation.

questions.topic: Where the sixty-name cycle comes from
questions.stem: If you have ten stems and twelve branches, how many unique names result?
questions.explanation: Parity reduction gives 60. The tempting 120 answer ignores the pairing rule.

questions.topic: Why one hundred and twenty pairings give sixty names
questions.stem: What would happen if parity were ignored in the cycle?

answer.exemplar: If parity were ignored, all 120 pairings would appear, breaking the traditional sixty-name cycle and the alignment of stems with branches.

questions.explanation: Ignoring parity doubles the names. The tempting no-change answer ignores the rule's role.

questions.topic: A name that comes round again after sixty years
questions.stem: A person born in a certain cycle year wants the next same-named year. When is it?
questions.explanation: The name returns after 60 years. The tempting 30-year answer halves the cycle.

questions.topic: Naming a modern year in the cycle

stimulus.body: Someone names a modern year by counting stems and branches from year 1 CE without checking a reference point.

questions.stem: Is this method reliable?

options.text: No, because an anchor year is needed

options.misconception: ignores the need for a reference

options.text: Yes, because year 1 CE is the anchor
No, because modern years have no names

questions.explanation: An anchor year is needed. The tempting counting-only answer ignores the offset.

questions.topic: The cycle name of a revolution year
questions.stem: If 1911 and 1949 are 38 years apart, do they share a cycle name?

options.text: Yes, because both are revolution years
options.misconception: confuses event type with cycle name

options.text: No, because 38 is not a multiple of 60
No, because modern years are unnamed

questions.explanation: 38 is not a multiple of 60, so names differ. The tempting yes answer confuses event type with cycle.

questions.topic: The cycle name shared by two twentieth-century years
questions.stem: How many years apart are two years sharing a cycle name, at minimum?
questions.explanation: The minimum gap is 60 years. The tempting 30 answer halves the cycle.

questions.topic: The branches as two-hour periods

stimulus.body: A text says each branch covers exactly one hour, so twelve branches fill twelve hours of a day.

questions.stem: Is this claim accurate?

options.text: Yes, because twelve branches fit twelve hours
No, because each branch covers two hours

questions.explanation: Each branch covers two hours. The tempting twelve-hours answer confuses branches with hours.

questions.topic: How the twelve periods fill a day
questions.stem: If a day has 24 hours and each period is 2 hours, how many periods fit?
questions.explanation: 24 divided by 2 is 12. The tempting 24 answer forgets to divide.

questions.topic: The animal attached to each branch
questions.stem: Why is the animal a mnemonic rather than a literal attribute?

answer.exemplar: The animal is a mnemonic because it helps people remember the branch, not because the branch literally embodies that animal's traits.

questions.explanation: Animals aid memory, not literal traits. The tempting literal answer confuses symbol with reality.

questions.topic: The branches as month names
questions.stem: If twelve branches name twelve months, which month corresponds to the first branch?
questions.explanation: The first branch maps to the first month. The tempting seventh answer offsets wrongly.

questions.topic: Why the twenty-four terms are fifteen degrees apart
questions.stem: How many degrees does the sun move between two solar terms spaced 15 degrees apart after three terms?
questions.explanation: Three terms times 15 degrees equals 45 degrees. The tempting 15 answer forgets to multiply.
